did_you_know.text: Did you know? The prophet compares Israel to a vine: the more fruit it produced, the more altars and sacred pillars it made. Material prosperity did not lead to faithful worship of the Lord, but to the spread of foreign forms of worship.

Did you know? The expression “their hearts are divided” describes a divided heart and incomplete loyalty. According to the verse, this division leads to guilt and to the destruction of the altars and sacred pillars.

Did you know? Israel is described as saying, “We have no king,” because the people do not fear the Lord. The verse links rejecting the Lord’s authority with a lack of trust in political leadership as well.

Did you know? “The calves of Beth-aven” is a negative name for the calf at Bethel. The prophet describes the people of Samaria and the priests mourning the loss of the calf idol and the dishonor brought upon it.

Did you know? According to the verse, the calf of Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria as part of the plunder or as a tribute to the king called “Jareb.” Thus, the idol once regarded as a source of religious pride is presented as an object taken by an enemy.

Did you know? The prophet calls the high places “the high places of wickedness” and predicts that they will be destroyed. In response to their terror and shame, the people will ask the mountains and hills to hide them.

Did you know? Israel is compared to a trained heifer that loves to thresh. The image combines criticism with the possibility of correction: Israel is capable of useful work, but the Lord will soon place a heavier yoke on them.

Did you know? In the midst of the prophecy of disaster comes a call to repentance: to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, plow new ground, and seek the Lord until he comes and pours righteousness upon them.

Did you know? The verse presents a direct contrast to the call in the previous verse: instead of plowing righteousness, Israel plowed wickedness and reaped injustice. They also trusted in their own way and their warriors instead of relying on the Lord’s help.

Did you know? The destruction of the fortresses is described by comparing it to the sack of Beth-arbel, where a mother was crushed with her children. The image emphasizes the violence and devastation that await Israel.
